# Losing the Night

At 4:31 on the morning of January 17, 1994, an earthquake measuring 6.7 struck beneath the San Fernando Valley, snapping power lines and plunging Los Angeles into sudden darkness. In the eerie quiet after the shaking stopped, residents who stumbled outside saw something vast and faint arched over the city: a river of pale light, dusted with grain, running horizon to horizon. According to astronomers at the Griffith Observatory, the phones started ringing. Callers wanted to know what the giant silvery cloud was, and whether it posed any danger. It was the Milky Way—the galaxy we live inside, viewed edge-on from within—a sight every human being had shared for a hundred thousand years, and which many Angelenos had somehow never had.

The anecdote usually gets told as a joke about clueless city people. It isn't funny. It's a report from a crime scene. Something was taken—quietly, fixture by fixture, decade by decade—and the theft was so complete that its victims didn't know what they'd been robbed of. They looked up into a hole in the sky and, not knowing it was a hole, called it a cloud.

For nearly the entire history of our species, night meant real darkness. Not the dim darkness of a modern suburb, where the sky never quite goes black, but darkness that fell like a verdict: darkness in which the landscape disappeared and the sky became the brightest thing in the world. Under those conditions, the stars were not decoration. They were infrastructure. The Milky Way was the single most conspicuous object in the night of every human who ever lived until roughly the era of our grandparents. Every culture named it. The Greeks saw Hera's spilled milk and gave us the word *galaxy* from it. Chinese astronomers called it the Silver River, separating the star of the Weaver Girl from her Cowherd on opposite banks. The San people of the Kalahari called it the Backbone of Night. And some Aboriginal Australian nations read the dark rifts running along the Milky Way's length as an Emu in the Sky—a constellation made not of stars but of shadow itself, a figure drawn in the negative space. Under skies we no longer have, observers swear the Milky Way is bright enough to cast a faint shadow of its own.

From that river of light, humanity built its first sciences. Astronomy is the oldest of them for a reason: the sky was the original clock, calendar, and scripture. The moon's phases gave us the month. The wandering planets and the wheel of constellations gave us the year and its festivals. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean reading the rising and setting points of stars, holding entire continents of knowledge in memory. The date of Easter still hides a full moon inside it; Ramadan still begins with a sighting. We are, all of us, descended from people who knew the night sky the way modern city dwellers know traffic signals.

Darkness shaped not just our cultures but our bodies. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, court records, medical texts, and prayer books from the preindustrial world, discovered something strange: for centuries, Western sleep came in two acts. People went to bed shortly after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours—the "first sleep"—then woke naturally around midnight and stayed awake for an hour or so before returning to the "second sleep." The interval had a name in dozens of languages: French *premier sommeil*, Italian *primo sonno*. It was a recognized hour of its own, used for prayer, for reflecting on dreams, for talking quietly by the fire, for making love. Court records even capture burglars plying their trade in the gap between sleeps. The word *midnight* makes sense only in a world where night had a middle you were sometimes awake to see.

The sleep researcher Thomas Wehr later ran an experiment that amounts to an archaeology of the body. He gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness every night for a month—mimicking the light schedule of a winter in a preindustrial world—and their sleep quietly reorganized itself into the old pattern: a block of deep sleep, a calm and contemplative hour of wakefulness, another block of sleep. The hour between wasn't insomnia. It looked like a feature, something the body does when the dark lasts long enough. We didn't merely lose the night. We changed what sleep is.

Then we lit the world. In 1807, London's Pall Mall became one of the first streets anywhere glowing with gaslight; before that, the desperate hired linkboys—children with flaming torches—to walk them home through the black. Paris, the so-called City of Light, blazed next. Edison's Pearl Street station switched on lower Manhattan in 1882. And after the Second World War, cheap electricity met cheap fixtures and the flood began in earnest: billboards, ballparks, strip malls, stadiums, parking lots lit like operating theaters at 2 a.m.

The result is measured by satellites, which is its own dark joke—the view of our lights from space is now better than our view of the stars from the ground. The 2016 world atlas of artificial night sky brightness found that more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies; in the United States and Europe, it's 99 percent. About a third of all people alive—including roughly 80 percent of North Americans—cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. And it's accelerating. A 2023 study drawing on a decade of citizen-scientist star counts concluded that skyglow is brightening about 9.6 percent per year. The authors put it in human terms: a child born where 250 stars are visible tonight would see only about 100 from the same spot by their eighteenth birthday.

The culprit is mostly *skyglow*—light thrown upward or sideways that scatters off air and aerosols and returns as a luminous fog. Stand on a ridge a hundred miles from a major city on a clear night and you can still see its dome, a pale blister on the horizon, the ghost of a million bad fixtures. Add glare, light trespass, and clutter, and you have the full catastrophe: not darkness's absence but its occupation.

We lit the world without asking what the darkness was for. Other species hadn't finished answering either. Consider the sea turtle, whose hatchlings emerge from the sand on Florida beaches and instinctively race toward the brightest horizon—which, for a hundred million years, meant the moonlit sea. Now it often means a strip mall behind the dunes, and thousands of hatchlings a year march inland to die on highways and in pools. Towns that darken their beaches during nesting season watch the hatchlings find the water again. Consider the September 11 Tribute in Light in Manhattan, whose twin beams turned out to be an unplanned ecological experiment: researchers estimated the beams trapped more than a million migrating birds across the nights studied—songbirds circling in the light like moths, burning fuel they needed to fly on. The organizers now switch the beams off for about twenty minutes at a stretch whenever monitoring shows large numbers of birds circling, and the birds pour out of the beams and resume their journey. Consider the insects: a British study found that streetlights cut caterpillar numbers in hedgerows roughly in half, and moths—the night's great pollinators—are lured into streetlights to circle until they die of exhaustion or predation. Fireflies court with light, and we have drowned the conversation. Even coral reefs sense the moon: spawning is synchronized to its cycle, and experiments show that artificial night light can scramble the timing, desynchronizing an event that depends on every reef doing it at once.

We're not exempt. Nighttime light suppresses melatonin, and blue-rich white LEDs—the kind we've blanketed the world in over the past decade—are the most potent kind. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies shift work involving circadian disruption as probably carcinogenic to humans. Chronic exposure to light at night is linked to sleep disorders, metabolic disease, depression. We took a rhythm our bodies kept for a hundred thousand years and broke it in three generations.

None of this is an argument for a world of darkness, and honesty requires saying so. Light at night is a genuine good: it means safety, emergency rooms, the teenager walking home, the simple pleasure of a lit street. The problem is not light. The problem is waste and thoughtlessness—light that spills where it does no good, aimed where nothing needs seeing, burning all night where no one is awake. By some estimates, a third of outdoor lighting in the United States is thrown straight into the sky, at a cost of billions of dollars a year, illuminating nothing but air. And the safety argument for that waste is weaker than it looks. When English councils switched off or dimmed streetlights in natural experiments across dozens of areas, researchers found no significant increase in crime or traffic accidents. Meanwhile, poorly designed lighting can make things worse: an overlit parking lot creates glare that blinds you to everything outside the beam, and blacker shadows at its edges. Good lighting, it turns out, is not more light. It's shielded, warm-colored, aimed at the ground, and off when nobody needs it.

Here is what moves me most about all of this: the loss was never chosen, and the reversal costs almost nothing. No parliament ever voted to remove the Milky Way from the sky. It vanished as an externality, accumulating one unshielded fixture at a time, each decision individually reasonable—a safer parking lot, a brighter storefront—while the sum of all of them erased the oldest shared experience of our species. Every environmental loss we usually mourn has the same shape and a terrible asymmetry: the carbon takes centuries to recapture, the extinct species never comes back, the ozone hole closes on the scale of decades. Skyglow heals at the speed of a light switch. The moment the lights come down—or are aimed down—the sky above any town returns to something like what it was for Galileo. Of all the wounds we've inflicted on the natural world, this is the only one that closes overnight. We polluted the night with something as easy to stop as light. There is something both comic and consoling in that, and more than a little shaming: the stars are not gone. They are merely hidden behind our carelessness, and carelessness is reversible.

Which is why the hope here is more than rhetoric. Flagstaff, Arizona—protecting the observatory where Pluto was discovered—passed America's first lighting ordinance in 1958 and became the world's first certified Dark Sky City in 2001. More than two hundred places worldwide, from Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand to entire counties in the American Southwest, have earned Dark Sky certification by shielding fixtures, capping brightness, and embracing curfews. France now requires most non-essential shop and office lights to go out overnight. Amber, full-cutoff lighting lets Florida hatchlings find the sea. Even the pandemic, for all its horror, gave a glimpse: with traffic stilled, skyglow measurably thinned, and there are photographs from locked-down cities of Venus blazing over empty avenues. The barrier was never technological. It's attention. Nobody misses a night sky they've never seen; each generation's baseline quietly erodes, the way we stopped missing quiet when we stopped hearing it.

So here is the whole prescription, or the beginning of one: go find out what was stolen. Drive an hour or two beyond the glow of any city, on a clear moonless night, and then wait—this is the crucial part, and the hard one—because your eyes need the better part of half an hour to adapt, and a single glance at a phone screen will undo most of it. Stand in a field. Let the darkness become total. And then look up.

What you will see first is not faintness but abundance, a shock of it: the Milky Way not as a smudge but as a structure, a luminous river with dark channels running through it, so bright it seems it should hum. You are seeing the disk of your own galaxy from the inside, from the outskirts of an unremarkable spiral arm, light from a hundred billion suns arriving all at once across distances your brain will refuse to convert into miles. Every person you've read about in a history book saw this. Every one of them. It was the common inheritance of every human being who ever lived, and you have to drive two hours and switch off your phone to collect it.

The stars did not go out. They are exactly where they have always been, waiting behind the glare, patient in a way that shames us. Last time Los Angeles saw them, it took an earthquake to turn out the lights. It shouldn't take one next time. The darkness isn't the enemy, and never was—it's the backdrop against which the whole human story happened, the canvas under which we learned to keep time, tell stories, and wonder what we were. It costs nothing to give it back. The stars only ask that we stop shining so much at the ground, and look up.
